patient.chief_complaint: Episodic right hand clenching and difficulty with speech and fine hand movements
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Delgado is a 28-year-old right-handed woman who presents to the emergency department after experiencing a second episode of involuntary right hand clenching followed by transient difficulty with speech and fine motor movements in her right hand. Today's episode occurred approximately 2 hours prior to arrival while she was studying at home. She noted a sudden involuntary tonic posturing of her right hand lasting approximately 30 seconds, followed by difficulty typing on her laptop and mild slurring of her speech that persisted for roughly 15 minutes before gradually improving. She reports a similar but briefer episode approximately 2 weeks ago while at volleyball practice, which she initially attributed to muscle cramps and fatigue and did not seek medical attention. Notably, approximately 3 weeks prior to today's presentation, she sustained a direct impact to the left side of her neck from a volleyball during practice. She experienced mild neck pain and stiffness for a few days afterward but did not seek medical evaluation as the pain resolved with over-the-counter analgesics. She denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, or generalized seizure activity during either episode. She has no history of seizures or epilepsy. She denies any recent febrile illness, weight loss, night sweats, skin rashes, or joint pain. She has not traveled recently and has no history of trauma other than the volleyball incident. Her partner, who witnessed today's episode, confirms the description and notes that she appeared fully conscious throughout, though she seemed frustrated by her difficulty speaking. The patient is particularly concerned because she needs full use of her right hand for laboratory work in her graduate program.

results.title: Cervical Artery Dissection in Stroke Study (CADISS Trial)
results.authors: Markus HS, Hayter E, et al.
results.key_finding: No significant difference between antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy for preventing stroke and death in patients with cervical artery dissection. Recurrent stroke rate was low in both groups.

results.title: Cervical artery dissection: Current concepts and management
results.key_finding: Cervical artery dissection accounts for approximately 20% of ischemic strokes in young adults. Trauma (including minor or sports-related) is a recognized precipitant. Antithrombotic therapy is recommended for at least 3-6 months.

results.title: AHA/ASA Scientific Statement on Cervical Artery Dissections
results.authors: Biller J, Sacco RL, et al.
results.key_finding: For extracranial carotid or vertebral artery dissection, antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) for at least 3-6 months is reasonable. Screening for underlying connective tissue disorders is recommended.

output.summary: Current evidence from the CADISS trial shows no significant difference between anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy for secondary stroke prevention in cervical artery dissection. Both are considered acceptable approaches. Antithrombotic therapy is recommended for 3-6 months with follow-up vascular imaging to assess for recanalization. Cervical artery dissection is a leading cause of stroke in young adults, and minor trauma (including sports injuries) is a recognized risk factor. Screening for connective tissue disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, Loeys-Dietz syndromes) is recommended.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT MUST exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered (tPA decision modeled here through drug-interaction/contraindication check).
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be reviewed before IV thrombolysis to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy contraindications.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Recognize neck/face/eye pain preceding focal deficit as a dissection alert
Pursue cervical vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) to confirm dissection
Initiate antiplatelet or anticoagulation per CADISS for 3-6 months
Evaluate for and treat focal motor seizures if EEG or clinical features support concurrent epileptic activity
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not skip dedicated cervical vessel imaging in a young stroke patient — dissection is the leading mechanism
Do not anchor on functional or migraine diagnoses in the face of objective infarct and dissection findings
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Cervical arterial dissection is the most common stroke etiology in young adults; neck/face pain and prior trauma raise pretest probability
Stereotyped focal motor episodes can coexist with ischemic stroke (irritative cortical focus from infarct) — EEG can clarify
T1 fat-saturated MRI of the neck reveals intramural hematoma — the diagnostic hallmark
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
